An evidence-based analysis of 14,533 marketplace listings

Six syllabus modules, one real dataset (VIDA-NYU/LTS). Every number on this page was computed by analysis.py; nothing is hand-entered.

00

Dataset & Scope

What was analysed and why

14,533shark-trophy eBay listings, 2024-07-02 to 2024-07-12; 801 labelled positive
152,495unlabelled leather-product listings (price outliers, data quality)
999human-labelled validation rows (499 shark, 500 leather)

The dataset comes from a paper on detecting wildlife trafficking in online marketplaces. The primary table is shark_trophy.csv (title, description, price, seller location, retrieval time, binary label). The syllabus (Applied Data Science, B.Tech Computer Engineering) defines the tasks: Module 1 process and validation, 2 descriptive statistics, 3 inferential statistics, 4 regression, 5 anomaly detection, 6 time series.

Introduction to Data Science

Data, process, preparation, validation

LO 1.1LO 1.2LO 1.3LO 1.4

Task 1.1 — Data profiling and preparation

Objective

Understand volume, dimensionality and quality of the wildlife-trafficking listing data before any modelling (Contents 1.1–1.3).

Methodology

Load all CSVs, count rows/columns/types, check missing values and duplicates, clean titles (strip the “| eBay” suffix), engineer numeric features, and de-duplicate titles for the ML copy so identical listings cannot leak across folds.

Implementation

Show implementation (analysis.py › M1)
sh["title_clean"] = sh.title.str.replace(r"\s*\|\s*eBay$", "", regex=True).str.strip()
sh["t"] = pd.to_datetime(sh.retrieved, utc=True)
sh["country"] = sh.location.fillna("Unknown").str.split(",").str[-1].str.strip()
sh["is_us"] = (sh.country == "United States").astype(int)
sh["title_len"] = sh.title_clean.str.len(); sh["n_words"] = sh.title_clean.str.split().str.len()
sh["upper_ratio"] = sh.title_clean.apply(lambda s: sum(c.isupper() for c in s) / max(1, sum(c.isalpha() for c in s)))
sh["has_digit"] = sh.title_clean.str.contains(r"\d").astype(int)
sh["desc_len"] = sh.description.fillna("").str.len(); sh["log_desc"] = np.log1p(sh.desc_len)
sh["log_price"] = np.log(sh.price)
low = sh.title_clean.str.lower()
sh["kw_jaw"] = low.str.contains("jaw").astype(int); sh["kw_tooth"] = low.str.contains("tooth|teeth").astype(int)
sh["kw_fossil"] = low.str.contains("fossil|megalodon").astype(int)
dup_title = int(sh.title_clean.duplicated().sum())
conflict = int((sh.groupby("title_clean").label.nunique() > 1).sum())
R["m1"] = dict(rows=len(sh), cols=sh.shape[1] - 0, leather_rows=len(lea), leather_cols=lea.shape[1],
               shark_val_rows=len(sval), leather_val_rows=len(lval),
               dtypes_numeric=int(sh.select_dtypes("number").shape[1]), missing=sh[["image", "location"]].isna().sum().to_dict(),
               dup_urls=int(sh.url.duplicated().sum()), dup_titles=dup_title, conflicting_dup_titles=conflict,
               pos=int(sh.label.sum()), pos_rate=float(sh.label.mean()),
               t_min=str(sh.t.min()), t_max=str(sh.t.max()), sellers=int(sh.seller.nunique()),
               memory_mb=float(sh.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6), leather_memory_mb=float(lea.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6))
# modelling copy: de-duplicate titles so identical listings cannot leak between folds
ml = sh.drop_duplicates("title_clean").reset_index(drop=True)
R["m1"]["ml_rows"] = len(ml); R["m1"]["ml_pos"] = int(ml.label.sum())
def text_lr(cw=None): return Pipeline([("tf", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=5, sublinear_tf=True, max_features=20000)),
                                       ("lr", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight=cw, random_state=SEED))])
X, y = ml.title_clean, ml.label.values
skf = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
cv = cross_validate(text_lr(), X, y, cv=skf, scoring=["f1", "average_precision", "precision", "recall"])
R["m1"]["kfold"] = {k: [float(v) for v in cv[f"test_{k}"]] for k in ["f1", "average_precision", "precision", "recall"]}
# Bootstrap: refit on resampled training rows, score on out-of-bag rows (B=100)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=SEED)
Xtr = Xtr.reset_index(drop=True); boot = []
for b in range(100):
    idx = rng.integers(0, len(Xtr), len(Xtr)); oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(Xtr)), idx)
    m = text_lr().fit(Xtr.iloc[idx], ytr[idx]); boot.append(f1_score(ytr[oob], m.predict(Xtr.iloc[oob])))
R["m1"]["boot_f1"] = dict(mean=float(np.mean(boot)), lo=float(np.percentile(boot, 2.5)), hi=float(np.percentile(boot, 97.5)), B=100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
ax[0].bar(range(1, 6), R["m1"]["kfold"]["f1"], color=PAL["teal"]); ax[0].axhline(np.mean(R["m1"]["kfold"]["f1"]), color=PAL["orange"], ls="--")
ax[0].set(title="5-fold stratified CV: F1 per fold", xlabel="fold", ylabel="F1", ylim=(0, 1))
ax[1].hist(boot, bins=18, color=PAL["pink"]); ax[1].set(title="Bootstrap (B=100) out-of-bag F1", xlabel="F1")
save("m1_validation")

Results

14,533shark listings (11 raw columns)
152,495leather listings
5.5%positive (shark-product) rate
7,013distinct sellers
CheckResult
Shark file in memory / leather file in memory49 MB / 136 MB
Missing values (shark)image: 7, location: 2
Duplicate URLs / duplicate titles0 / 8 (conflicting labels among duplicates: 0)
Retrieval window2024-07-02 → 2024-07-12
Modelling copy after title de-duplication14,525 rows, 801 positive

Interpretation

The data is high-volume and mixed-type: free text (titles), numeric (price), categorical (country, seller) and timestamps. The classes are strongly imbalanced (about 1 in 18 listings is positive), which dictates metric choice (F1 and average precision rather than accuracy) and motivates the SMOTE comparison in Module 5. Very few duplicates exist, so leakage risk is small but was removed anyway.

Task 1.2 — Model building with k-fold cross-validation and bootstrapping

Objective

Build a baseline text classifier for “is this listing a shark product?” and estimate how well it generalises (Content 1.4, LO 1.4).

Methodology

TF-IDF (1–2-grams) + logistic regression on the cleaned title. Stratified 5-fold CV for F1, precision, recall, average precision. A bootstrap (B = 100) refits on resampled training rows and scores on the out-of-bag rows to get a percentile interval.

Implementation

Implemented in the M1 chunk shown in Task 1.1.

Results

0.722CV F1 (mean)
0.967CV precision
0.577CV recall
0.861CV avg. precision

Bootstrap out-of-bag F1: mean 0.707, 95% percentile interval [0.654, 0.752].

Interpretation

Performance is stable across folds (F1 0.70–0.77) and the bootstrap interval is consistent with it. The model is highly precise but misses many positives (precision 0.97 vs recall 0.58). Accuracy would have looked excellent (about 94.5%) simply by predicting “negative”, which is why it is not used. Not performed: leave-one-out CV (14.5k refits of a text pipeline was judged impractical and k-fold is the standard substitute at this size).

Data science vs. data analytics (Content 1.5–1.6)

Here, analytics is the descriptive/inferential work of Modules 2–3 (what does the market look like, are groups different?), while data science adds predictive and automated components: classifiers, regression, anomaly detectors and forecasts (Modules 4–6) evaluated with held-out data. The application domain is wildlife-trade triage: scanning large marketplace crawls for illegal animal products.

Data Exploration: Descriptive Statistics

Centre, spread, shape and visual analytics

Task 2.1 — Univariate exploration

Objective

Summarise price and title characteristics: central tendency, spread, symmetry, skewness and kurtosis (Contents 2.1–2.3, LO 2.1–2.3).

Methodology

Mean/median/mode, SD, IQR, CV; Karl Pearson’s coefficient 3(mean − median)/SD; Bowley’s quartile coefficient; moment skewness and excess kurtosis. Price is also analysed on a log scale.

Implementation

Show implementation (analysis.py › M2)
def describe(s):
    s = pd.Series(s).dropna(); q1, q2, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .5, .75])
    sd = s.std()
    return dict(n=int(len(s)), mean=s.mean(), median=q2, mode=float(s.round(2).mode().iloc[0]), std=sd, var=s.var(), min=s.min(), max=s.max(),
                range=s.max() - s.min(), q1=q1, q3=q3, iqr=q3 - q1, cv=sd / s.mean(),
                pearson_skew=3 * (s.mean() - q2) / sd,                     # Karl Pearson's 2nd coefficient
                bowley=(q3 + q1 - 2 * q2) / (q3 - q1),                      # Bowley's quartile coefficient
                moment_skew=stats.skew(s), excess_kurtosis=stats.kurtosis(s))
R["m2"] = {c: {k: float(v) for k, v in describe(sh[c]).items()} for c in ["price", "log_price", "title_len", "n_words", "desc_len"]}
num = ["log_price", "title_len", "n_words", "upper_ratio", "log_desc", "is_us", "label"]
corr = sh[num].corr(); R["m2"]["corr"] = corr.round(3).to_dict()
r, p = stats.pearsonr(sh.title_len, sh.log_price); rs, ps = stats.spearmanr(sh.title_len, sh.log_price)
R["m2"]["title_len_vs_logprice"] = dict(pearson=r, p=p, spearman=rs, p_s=ps)
R["m2"]["by_label"] = sh.groupby("label").agg(n=("price", "size"), median_price=("price", "median"), mean_price=("price", "mean"),
                                              median_len=("title_len", "median")).round(2).reset_index().to_dict("records")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.6))
ax[0].hist(sh.price.clip(upper=sh.price.quantile(.99)), bins=50, color=PAL["orange"]); ax[0].set(title="Price (clipped at 99th pct)", xlabel="USD")
sns.histplot(sh.log_price, bins=50, kde=True, color=PAL["teal"], ax=ax[1]); ax[1].set(title="log(price)", xlabel="ln USD")
sns.histplot(sh.title_len, bins=40, color=PAL["pink"], ax=ax[2]); ax[2].set(title="Title length", xlabel="characters")
save("m2_hist")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.8))
sns.violinplot(data=sh, x="label", y="log_price", palette=[PAL["teal"], PAL["orange"]], ax=ax[0]); ax[0].set_title("log(price) by label (violin)")
sns.boxplot(data=sh, x="label", y="title_len", palette=[PAL["teal"], PAL["orange"]], ax=ax[1]); ax[1].set_title("Title length by label (box)")
sns.boxenplot(data=sh, x="label", y="log_desc", palette=[PAL["teal"], PAL["orange"]], ax=ax[2]); ax[2].set_title("log(1+description length) (boxen)")
save("m2_violin_box")
s = sh.sample(4000, random_state=SEED)
plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.2)); sns.scatterplot(data=s, x="title_len", y="log_price", hue="label", palette=[PAL["teal"], PAL["orange"]], alpha=.55, s=14)
plt.title("Title length vs log(price)"); save("m2_scatter")
g = sns.pairplot(sh.sample(1500, random_state=SEED)[["log_price", "title_len", "n_words", "log_desc", "label"]], hue="label",

g.figure.savefig(f"{FIG}/m2_pairplot.png", dpi=100); plt.close("all")
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4.6)); sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="PuOr_r", center=0, square=True, cbar=False); plt.title("Pearson correlation heatmap")
save("m2_heatmap")
top = sh.country.value_counts().head(8).index
b = sh[sh.country.isin(top)].groupby("country").agg(n=("price", "size"), med=("price", "median"), pos=("label", "sum")).reset_index()

plt.figure(figsize=(7.5, 4.4)); plt.scatter(b.n, b.med, s=b.pos_rate * 9000 + 40, c=PAL["pink"], alpha=.6, edgecolor=PAL["plum"])
for _, rw in b.iterrows(): plt.annotate(rw.country, (rw.n, rw.med), ha="center", fontsize=8)

Results

VariableMeanMedianModeSDIQRPearson skewBowleyMoment skewExcess kurt.
Price (USD)177.9725.009.991367.3356.010.340.5728.661097.3
ln(price)3.493.222.301.421.670.570.220.851.7
Title length69.2875.0080.0013.6615.00-1.26-0.47-1.512.0
Words in title11.2912.0012.002.563.00-0.84-0.33-0.690.7

Interpretation

Raw price is extremely right-skewed: mean $178 vs median $25, moment skewness 28.7, excess kurtosis 1,097. Note that Karl Pearson’s coefficient is only 0.34 here because it uses the median and divides by an SD inflated by the extreme tail, so it badly understates this skew; Bowley’s coefficient (0.57) and the moment skewness agree on positive skew. After the log transform, skew drops to 0.85 with modest kurtosis (1.7). Title length is mildly left-skewed, capped by eBay’s 80-character limit.

Interpretation

Title length and ln(price) are essentially uncorrelated (Pearson r = 0.026, Spearman ρ = 0.033; statistically detectable only because n is large). Task 3.1 — Distributions: Normal, CLT and Poisson

Objective

Check which standard distributions describe the data (LO 3.1).

Methodology

Shapiro–Wilk / D’Agostino tests and Q-Q plot for ln(price); a simulation of the Central Limit Theorem on the raw price (3,000 resamples at n = 5, 30, 300); a Poisson goodness-of-fit (dispersion) check on hourly listing-retrieval counts.

Implementation

Show implementation (analysis.py › M3)
lp = sh.log_price
samp = lp.sample(5000, random_state=SEED)
R["m3"] = dict(shapiro_W=float(stats.shapiro(samp)[0]), shapiro_p=float(stats.shapiro(samp)[1]),
               dagostino_p=float(stats.normaltest(lp)[1]), mu=float(lp.mean()), sigma=float(lp.std()))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.8)); stats.probplot(lp, plot=ax[0]); ax[0].set_title("Q-Q plot: log(price)")
xs = np.linspace(lp.min(), lp.max(), 200); ax[1].hist(lp, bins=50, density=True, color=PAL["teal"], alpha=.7)
ax[1].plot(xs, stats.norm.pdf(xs, lp.mean(), lp.std()), color=PAL["orange"], lw=2); ax[1].set_title("Normal fit to log(price)"); save("m3_normal")
# Central Limit Theorem on the (very right-skewed) raw price
clt = {}; fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.2))
ax[0].hist(sh.price.clip(upper=500), bins=50, color=PAL["orange"]); ax[0].set_title("Population (clip 500)")
for a, n in zip(ax[1:], [5, 30, 300]):
    means = np.array([rng.choice(sh.price.values, n).mean() for _ in range(3000)]); clt[n] = dict(skew=float(stats.skew(means)), sd=float(means.std()))
    a.hist(means.clip(max=np.percentile(means, 99.5)), bins=40, color=PAL["teal"]); a.set_title(f"Sample means, n={n}")
R["m3"]["clt"] = clt; R["m3"]["pop_skew"] = float(stats.skew(sh.price)); save("m3_clt")
# Confidence intervals
def tci(x): m, se = x.mean(), stats.sem(x); lo, hi = stats.t.interval(.95, len(x) - 1, m, se); return dict(mean=float(m), lo=float(lo), hi=float(hi))
R["m3"]["ci_price"] = tci(sh.price); R["m3"]["ci_logprice"] = tci(lp)
R["m3"]["ci_geo_price"] = {k: float(np.exp(v)) for k, v in R["m3"]["ci_logprice"].items()}
lo, hi = proportion_confint(sh.label.sum(), len(sh), method="wilson"); R["m3"]["ci_pos_rate"] = dict(p=float(sh.label.mean()), lo=float(lo), hi=float(hi))
# Z-test (two proportions): share of positives, US vs non-US
cnt = sh.groupby("is_us").label.agg(["sum", "count"]); z, pz = proportions_ztest(cnt["sum"].values, cnt["count"].values)
R["m3"]["ztest"] = dict(z=float(z), p=float(pz), p_nonus=float(cnt.loc[0, "sum"] / cnt.loc[0, "count"]), p_us=float(cnt.loc[1, "sum"] / cnt.loc[1, "count"]),
                        n_nonus=int(cnt.loc[0, "count"]), n_us=int(cnt.loc[1, "count"]))
# Welch t-test: log price, positive vs negative listings
a1, a0 = lp[sh.label == 1], lp[sh.label == 0]; tt = stats.ttest_ind(a1, a0, equal_var=False)
pooled = np.sqrt(((len(a1) - 1) * a1.var() + (len(a0) - 1) * a0.var()) / (len(a1) + len(a0) - 2)); d = (a1.mean() - a0.mean()) / pooled
R["m3"]["ttest"] = dict(t=float(tt.statistic), p=float(tt.pvalue), df=float(tt.df), mean1=float(a1.mean()), mean0=float(a0.mean()), cohen_d=float(d))
# One-way ANOVA: log price across top-5 countries
t5 = sh.country.value_counts().head(5).index; groups = [lp[sh.country == c] for c in t5]
F, pF = stats.f_oneway(*groups); H, pH = stats.kruskal(*groups); lev = stats.levene(*groups)
ssb = sum(len(g) * (g.mean() - lp[sh.country.isin(t5)].mean()) ** 2 for g in groups); sst = ((lp[sh.country.isin(t5)] - lp[sh.country.isin(t5)].mean()) ** 2).sum()
R["m3"]["anova"] = dict(countries=list(t5), F=float(F), p=float(pF), eta2=float(ssb / sst), kruskal_H=float(H), kruskal_p=float(pH), levene_p=float(lev.pvalue),
                        means={c: float(g.mean()) for c, g in zip(t5, groups)})
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.8)); sns.boxplot(data=sh[sh.country.isin(t5)], x="country", y="log_price", order=list(t5), palette="Set2"); plt.xticks(rotation=15); plt.title("ANOVA groups: log(price) by country"); save("m3_anova")
# Type-I error (permutation of labels) and Type-II error / power
perm_p = []
lab = sh.label.values; lv = lp.values
for _ in range(1000):
    pl = rng.permutation(lab); perm_p.append(stats.ttest_ind(lv[pl == 1], lv[pl == 0], equal_var=False).pvalue)
R["m3"]["type1_rate"] = float(np.mean(np.array(perm_p) < .05))
pw = TTestIndPower(); R["m3"]["power_observed"] = float(pw.power(abs(d), len(a1), .05, ratio=len(a0) / len(a1)))
R["m3"]["mde_d_80"] = float(pw.solve_power(None, len(a1), .05, .8, ratio=len(a0) / len(a1)))
# Poisson: hourly retrieval counts (see M6 for the series)
hc = sh.t.dt.floor("h").value_counts().sort_index(); full = hc.reindex(pd.date_range(hc.index.min(), hc.index.max(), freq="h"))
runs = (full.isna() != full.isna().shift()).cumsum(); best = max((g for _, g in full.groupby(runs) if not g.isna().iloc[0]), key=len)
ser = best.astype(float); lam = ser.mean()
R["m3"]["poisson"] = dict(n_hours=int(len(ser)), lam=float(lam), var=float(ser.var()), dispersion=float(ser.var() / lam))
R["m3"]["poisson"]["chi2_p"] = float(stats.chi2.sf((len(ser) - 1) * ser.var() / lam, len(ser) - 1))  # dispersion test

Results

CheckResult
Shapiro–Wilk (n = 5000 sample)W = 0.956, p < 0.001
Skewness of sample means (population skew = 28.7)n=5: 12.41 / n=30: 5.09 / n=300: 1.78
Poisson fit, hourly counts (94 h)mean 57.8, variance 1919, dispersion 33.2, p < 0.001

Interpretation

ln(price) is not exactly normal (formally rejected; it is mildly right-skewed with slightly heavy tails) but is far closer to normal than raw price, so it is used for parametric methods. The CLT is visible: sample-mean skew shrinks from 12.4 at n = 5 to 1.8 at n = 300, yet is still not normal at n = 300 because the raw price tail is so heavy. Hourly counts are not Poisson: the variance is about 33 times the mean (over-dispersion), consistent with crawler batching rather than independent arrivals.

Task 3.2 — Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests

Objective

Quantify uncertainty and test group differences (LO 3.2–3.4).

Methodology

95% t-intervals (price, ln price), Wilson interval for the positive rate; two-proportion Z-test (US vs non-US positive share); Welch t-test on ln(price) for positive vs negative listings with Cohen’s d; one-way ANOVA of ln(price) across the five largest seller countries, with Levene (equal variance) and Kruskal–Wallis (non-parametric) checks.

Implementation

Implemented in the M3 chunk above.

Results

QuantityEstimate95% CI
Mean price (USD)177.97[155.73, 200.20]
Geometric-mean price (USD)32.81[32.06, 33.58]
Positive rate5.51%[5.15%, 5.89%]
TestStatisticp-valueEffect
Two-proportion Z (US vs non-US positive share)z = -3.72< 0.0015.8% vs 3.7%
Welch t (ln price, positive vs negative)t = 12.69 (df 876)< 0.001means 4.17 vs 3.45; Cohen’s d = 0.51
One-way ANOVA (United States, China, United Kingdom, Japan, Australia)F = 75.1< 0.001η² = 0.021
Levene (equal variances)–< 0.001variances differ
Kruskal–WallisH = 301< 0.001agrees with ANOVA

Interpretation

The mean price CI is wide ([156, 200] USD) because of the heavy tail, whereas the geometric mean (≈ $33) is tightly estimated. Positive listings are priced significantly higher (medium effect, d = 0.51), and US listings are more likely to be positive than non-US ones. Country differences in price are statistically significant but small in size (η² ≈ 2% of variance), and since Levene rejects equal variances the ANOVA is backed by the Kruskal–Wallis result rather than relied on alone; Japan stands out as the high-priced group (mean ln price 5.08).

Task 3.3 — Type-I and Type-II errors

Objective

Show the meaning of α and power empirically (LO 3.4).

Methodology

Permute the labels 1,000 times and count how often the Welch t-test falsely rejects at α = 0.05 (empirical Type-I rate). Compute power for the observed effect and the minimum detectable effect size at 80% power with the actual group sizes.

Implementation

Implemented in the M3 chunk above.

Results

0.055empirical Type-I rate (target 0.05)
1.00power at observed d
0.10min. detectable d at 80% power

Interpretation

The test is well calibrated: under shuffled labels it rejects 5.5% of the time, close to the nominal 5%. With 801 vs 13,732 listings the test can detect effects as small as d ≈ 0.10, so the Type-II risk for the observed medium effect is negligible. The flip side is that with this much data almost any difference becomes “significant”, so effect sizes (d, η²) matter more than p-values.

04

Regression Analysis

Equation, error terms, fit, significance

LO 4.1LO 4.2LO 4.3LO 4.4LO 4.5LO 4.6

Task 4.1 — Simple to multiple regression for ln(price)

Objective

Build, compare and select regression models for price (LO 4.1–4.6).

Methodology

Four nested OLS models (statsmodels) on an 80% training split, evaluated on a 20% test split: A) title length only; B) + text-shape features; C) + label, US seller, description length; D) + keyword indicators. Fit measures: R², adjusted R², AIC/BIC, overall F-test, nested F-tests, t-tests per coefficient, and test-set MAE and MAPE on the USD scale (back-transformed with Duan’s smearing factor).

Implementation

Show implementation (analysis.py › M4)
tr, te = train_test_split(sh, test_size=.2, random_state=SEED)
forms = {"A: title_len": "log_price ~ title_len",
         "B: + text shape": "log_price ~ title_len + n_words + upper_ratio + has_digit",
         "C: + label, US, desc": "log_price ~ title_len + n_words + upper_ratio + has_digit + label + is_us + log_desc",
         "D: + keywords": "log_price ~ title_len + n_words + upper_ratio + has_digit + label + is_us + log_desc + kw_jaw + kw_tooth + kw_fossil"}
fits, rows = {}, []
for k, f in forms.items():
    m = smf.ols(f, tr).fit(); fits[k] = m; smear = np.mean(np.exp(m.resid)); pr = np.exp(m.predict(te)) * smear
    rows.append(dict(model=k, k=int(m.df_model), r2=m.rsquared, adj_r2=m.rsquared_adj, aic=m.aic, bic=m.bic, F=m.fvalue, F_p=m.f_pvalue,
                     test_r2_log=1 - ((te.log_price - m.predict(te)) ** 2).sum() / ((te.log_price - te.log_price.mean()) ** 2).sum(),
                     test_mae_usd=float(np.mean(np.abs(te.price - pr))), test_mape_pct=float(np.mean(np.abs((te.price - pr) / te.price)) * 100),
                     test_mae_log=float(np.mean(np.abs(te.log_price - m.predict(te))))))
R["m4"] = dict(table=rows, n_train=len(tr), n_test=len(te), baseline_mae_usd=float(np.mean(np.abs(te.price - tr.price.median()))),
               baseline_mape_pct=float(np.mean(np.abs((te.price - tr.price.median()) / te.price)) * 100))
best_k = min(rows, key=lambda r: r["aic"])["model"]; bm = fits[best_k]; R["m4"]["best"] = best_k
ci = bm.conf_int(); R["m4"]["coef"] = [dict(term=i, coef=float(bm.params[i]), se=float(bm.bse[i]), t=float(bm.tvalues[i]), p=float(bm.pvalues[i]),
                                          lo=float(ci.loc[i, 0]), hi=float(ci.loc[i, 1])) for i in bm.params.index]
R["m4"]["nested_F"] = {f"{a} -> {b_}": dict(F=float(anova_lm(fits[a], fits[b_]).iloc[1]["F"]), p=float(anova_lm(fits[a], fits[b_]).iloc[1]["Pr(>F)"]))
                       for a, b_ in zip(list(forms)[:-1], list(forms)[1:])}
R["m4"]["resid"] = dict(skew=float(stats.skew(bm.resid)), kurt=float(stats.kurtosis(bm.resid)), bp_p=float(sm.stats.diagnostic.het_breuschpagan(bm.resid, bm.model.exog)[1]),
                        dw=float(sm.stats.durbin_watson(bm.resid)))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.8))
ax[0].scatter(bm.fittedvalues, bm.resid, s=5, alpha=.3, color=PAL["teal"]); ax[0].axhline(0, color=PAL["orange"]); ax[0].set(title="Residuals vs fitted", xlabel="fitted", ylabel="residual")
stats.probplot(bm.resid, plot=ax[1]); ax[1].set_title("Residual Q-Q")
ax[2].scatter(te.log_price, bm.predict(te), s=5, alpha=.3, color=PAL["pink"]); ax[2].plot([0, 10], [0, 10], color=PAL["plum"]); ax[2].set(title="Test: actual vs predicted", xlabel="actual ln price", ylabel="predicted"); save("m4_residuals")
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.6)); mm = pd.DataFrame(rows); x = np.arange(len(mm)); plt.bar(x - .2, mm.adj_r2, .4, color=PAL["teal"], label="adj R²"); plt.bar(x + .2, mm.test_r2_log, .4, color=PAL["orange"], label="test R²")
plt.xticks(x, [r.split(":")[0] for r in mm.model]); plt.legend(); plt.title("Model comparison"); save("m4_compare")

Interpretation

Meaning of the parameters: the intercept (2.12) is the predicted ln-price of a title with all predictors at zero; each slope is the change in ln-price per unit holding the others fixed (partial coefficient), so exp(β)−1 is the % price change. Holding other terms constant, a positive (shark-product) listing is about 95% pricier, a title containing a digit about 60% pricier, and a title with “tooth/teeth” about 32% pricier; title length (p = 0.91) and US seller (p = 0.19) are not significant.

Honest assessment: every model is overall significant (F-test) and each added block improves AIC and passes its nested F-test, so Model D is selected by AIC; but it explains only 7.6% of ln-price variance (test R² 0.055). Price is mostly driven by things not in the title (item, size, condition, seller). In USD terms the model is worse than predicting the constant median (MAE $237 vs $168; MAPE 867% vs 125%), because MAE is minimised by the median and MAPE punishes over-prediction of very cheap items. The residuals are heteroscedastic (Breusch–Pagan p < 0.001), mildly right-skewed (skew 0.77), and not autocorrelated (Durbin–Watson 2.00), so the coefficient p-values should be read as indicative. The label is used as a regressor to describe association, not to claim causation.

Anomaly Detection

Outliers, causes, detection methods and SMOTE

Task 5.1 — Statistical, distance-based and density-based outlier detection

Objective

Detect unusual listings with several methods and compare them (LO 5.1–5.5, 5.7–5.8).

Methodology

Features: standardised ln(price), title length, word count. Methods: z-score (|z| > 3), Tukey IQR fences on ln(price), mean distance to 10 nearest neighbours (top 1%), Local Outlier Factor (contamination 1%), and DBSCAN noise points (eps = 0.35, min_samples = 10). Methods are compared by size, Jaccard overlap, and the positive rate among flagged listings.

Implementation

Show implementation (analysis.py › M5)
feat = StandardScaler().fit_transform(sh[["log_price", "title_len", "n_words"]]); flags = {}
zs = (lp - lp.mean()) / lp.std(); flags["z-score |z|>3"] = (zs.abs() > 3).values
q1, q3 = lp.quantile([.25, .75]); flags["IQR fence (log price)"] = ((lp < q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1)) | (lp > q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1))).values
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=11).fit(feat); dist = nn.kneighbors(feat)[0][:, 1:].mean(1); flags["kNN distance (top 1%)"] = dist > np.quantile(dist, .99)
flags["LOF (density, 1%)"] = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=.01).fit_predict(feat) == -1
flags["DBSCAN noise"] = DBSCAN(eps=.35, min_samples=10).fit_predict(feat) == -1
base = sh.label.mean(); R["m5"] = dict(methods={}, base_pos_rate=float(base))
for k, v in flags.items(): R["m5"]["methods"][k] = dict(n=int(v.sum()), pct=float(v.mean() * 100), pos_rate=float(sh.label[v].mean()) if v.sum() else None, lift=float(sh.label[v].mean() / base) if v.sum() else None)
names = list(flags); J = pd.DataFrame([[(flags[a] & flags[b]).sum() / max(1, (flags[a] | flags[b]).sum()) for b in names] for a in names], index=names, columns=names)
R["m5"]["jaccard"] = J.round(3).to_dict()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.6), sharey=True)
for a, k in zip(ax, ["z-score |z|>3", "kNN distance (top 1%)", "LOF (density, 1%)", "DBSCAN noise"]):
    a.scatter(sh.title_len, sh.log_price, s=3, color=PAL["teal"], alpha=.25); a.scatter(sh.title_len[flags[k]], sh.log_price[flags[k]], s=12, color=PAL["orange"]); a.set_title(f"{k}\n({flags[k].sum()} flagged)", fontsize=9); a.set_xlabel("title length")
ax[0].set_ylabel("ln price"); save("m5_methods")
R["m5"]["top_prices"] = sh.nlargest(6, "price")[["price", "title_clean"]].assign(title_clean=lambda d_: d_.title_clean.str[:70]).to_dict("records")

for k, pipe in cands.items():

Interpretation

The methods answer different questions: z-score/IQR look only at price, while kNN/LOF/DBSCAN also look at where a listing sits relative to others in the 3-D feature space, so overlap is partial (see Jaccard matrix). The IQR fence on ln(price) flags 3.2% of listings and those are 2.3× more likely than average to be positive; the distance/density flags are not enriched for positives (lift ≈ 0.75×), so a generic anomaly score is not a substitute for the classifier. Causes (Content 5.1), as visible in the data: the highest-priced listings are mostly off-topic search hits (cars, replica kits, industrial machinery) that entered the crawl through keyword matching, with one genuine shark-jaw listing among the top six; at the other end, placeholder prices such as $0.01 create low outliers. These causes come from reading the top-6 titles only; other flagged listings were not manually reviewed.

Task 5.3 — Class imbalance: SMOTE vs class weights vs plain

Objective

Evaluate whether synthetic oversampling helps detect the rare positive class (Content 5.6, LO 5.6; self-learning: F1, AUC-PR, confusion matrix).

Methodology

Three logistic-regression pipelines on TF-IDF features compared with stratified 5-fold CV and on a held-out 20% split. SMOTE is placed inside the CV pipeline so synthetic points are generated only from training folds. Metrics: precision, recall, F1, average precision (area under the PR curve), confusion matrix (TP/FP/FN/TN).

Implementation

Implemented in the M5 chunk above.

Results

ModelCV F1 ± SDCV precisionCV recallCV avg. precisionHold-out F1Hold-out APHold-out TP/FP/FN/TN
Plain LR0.722 ± 0.0280.9670.5770.8610.7010.87588/3/72/2742
Class-weighted LR0.742 ± 0.0140.6440.8780.8750.7770.890145/68/15/2677
SMOTE + LR0.743 ± 0.0150.6500.8680.8810.7710.898145/71/15/2674

Interpretation

Both imbalance remedies move the model from a high-precision / low-recall operating point (0.97 / 0.55) to a high-recall one (0.91 recall at 0.67 precision), cutting missed positives on the hold-out set from 72 to 15 at the cost of about 68 extra false alarms. In CV, F1 improves by only ≈ 0.021, about one fold-SD, and SMOTE is indistinguishable from simple class weighting (CV F1 0.743 vs 0.742). For triage, where missing a trafficked item is costlier than reviewing a false alarm, the high-recall variants are preferable, and the simpler class-weighted model is sufficient here.

06

Time Series Forecasting

Decomposition, smoothing, regression, ARIMA, error measures

LO 6.1LO 6.2LO 6.3LO 6.4LO 6.5LO 6.6

Task 6.1 — Decomposition, stationarity and forecasting

Objective

Apply the time-series toolkit to the only time-dependent signal in the data (LO 6.1–6.6).

Methodology

Series: number of listings retrieved per hour in the longest gap-free crawl run (94 hours, 2024-07-05 18:00:00 → 2024-07-09 15:00:00). Additive decomposition (period 24), ADF stationarity test, then 24-hour-ahead hold-out forecasts (train 70 h, test 24 h) from: overall average, moving average (w = 6), seasonal naive, simple exponential smoothing, linear-trend regression, and ARIMA (p,d,q ≤ (2,1,2) chosen by AIC). Metrics: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, MASE.

Implementation

Show implementation (analysis.py › M6)
ts = ser.copy(); ts.index = ts.index.tz_localize(None) if ts.index.tz is not None else ts.index
nte = 24; trn, tst = ts.iloc[:-nte], ts.iloc[-nte:]
adf = adfuller(trn); R["m6"] = dict(n=len(ts), start=str(ts.index[0]), end=str(ts.index[-1]), n_train=len(trn), n_test=len(tst), adf_stat=float(adf[0]), adf_p=float(adf[1]),
                                    mean=float(ts.mean()), sd=float(ts.std()))
dec = seasonal_decompose(ts, model="additive", period=24)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(9, 7), sharex=True)
for a, (n_, s_, c_) in zip(ax, [("Observed", dec.observed, "teal"), ("Trend", dec.trend, "orange"), ("Seasonal (24 h)", dec.seasonal, "pink"), ("Residual", dec.resid, "olive")]):
    a.plot(s_, color=PAL[c_]); a.set_ylabel(n_, fontsize=8)
save("m6_decomp")
R["m6"]["season_strength"] = float(max(0, 1 - np.nanvar(dec.resid) / np.nanvar(dec.seasonal + dec.resid)))
fc = {}; h = len(tst)
fc["Average (mean of train)"] = np.repeat(trn.mean(), h)
fc["Moving average (w=6)"] = np.repeat(trn.iloc[-6:].mean(), h)
fc["Seasonal naive (24 h)"] = trn.iloc[-24:].values[:h]
fc["Simple exp. smoothing"] = SimpleExpSmoothing(trn.values, initialization_method="estimated").fit().forecast(h)
t_ = np.arange(len(trn)); lr = np.polyfit(t_, trn.values, 1); fc["Linear trend regression"] = np.polyval(lr, np.arange(len(trn), len(trn) + h))
best_arima, best_aic = None, 1e18
for pdq in [(p, d_, q) for p in range(3) for d_ in range(2) for q in range(3)]:
    try:
        mm_ = ARIMA(trn.values, order=pdq).fit()
        if mm_.aic < best_aic: best_arima, best_aic, arm = pdq, mm_.aic, mm_
    except Exception: pass
fc[f"ARIMA{best_arima}"] = arm.forecast(h); R["m6"]["arima_order"] = list(best_arima); R["m6"]["arima_aic"] = float(best_aic)
mase_d = np.mean(np.abs(np.diff(trn.values))); met = []
for k, f_ in fc.items():
    e = tst.values - f_; met.append(dict(method=k, mae=float(np.mean(np.abs(e))), rmse=float(np.sqrt(np.mean(e ** 2))), mape=float(np.mean(np.abs(e / tst.values)) * 100), mase=float(np.mean(np.abs(e)) / mase_d)))
R["m6"]["metrics"] = met
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4)); plt.plot(trn.index, trn, color=PAL["plum"], label="train"); plt.plot(tst.index, tst, color="black", lw=2, label="actual")
for (k, f_), c in zip(fc.items(), [PAL["gold"], PAL["lime"], PAL["pink"], PAL["teal"], PAL["brown"], PAL["orange"]]): plt.plot(tst.index, f_, "--", color=c, label=k)
plt.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=2); plt.title("Hourly listings retrieved: 24-hour hold-out forecasts"); plt.ylabel("listings / hour"); save("m6_forecast")

json.dump(R, open("results.json", "w"), indent=1, default=lambda o: float(o) if isinstance(o, (np.floating, np.integer)) else str(o))
print("done")

Interpretation

The ADF test does not reject a unit root (p = 0.15), so the series is treated as non-stationary and ARIMA chose d = 1. The 24-hour seasonal component is modest (strength 0.38). No method forecasts well: the lowest MAE is 55.2 listings/hour for “Moving average (w=6)” against a series mean of 58, and all methods are within a few listings of each other, so the differences are not meaningful. MASE is above 6 for every method because it is scaled by the one-step naive error while these are 24-step forecasts, so it should be read as a relative scale, not a pass/fail. ARIMA (order chosen by AIC among the candidate orders) is not the best method on the hold-out.

Important limitation: this series measures how many listings the crawler retrieved per hour, not marketplace activity. The data spans only ~10 days with gaps, the usable gap-free run is 94 hours (about four daily cycles), and the hold-out is a single 24-hour window. The results demonstrate the methods and metrics on real data, but they should not be used to draw conclusions about wildlife-trade trends.

07

Limitations & Coverage

What was and was not done

Syllabus coverage

Syllabus contentEvidenceStatus

Limitations (read before citing any number)

  • Data access: the Google Drive folder could not be opened from the analysis environment. The four CSVs included in the public VIDA-NYU/LTS GitHub repository were used instead (shark_trophy, validation_sharks, data_leather, leather_validation). Any extra files only on Drive (e.g. the “animals” use case, images) were not analysed. Image columns were not used.
  • Labels: “label” comes from the dataset authors’ labelling process for shark products; its quality was not independently audited. The dataset contains marketplace listings, not confirmed illegal trade.
  • Short time span: shark listings were retrieved over ~10 days, and the time-series module uses crawl counts (a collection artefact) so it demonstrates technique rather than market behaviour.
  • Weak regression: price is barely explained by title features (R² ≈ 7%) and is not usable as a price predictor.
  • Mixed currencies / data errors in the leather file were identified but not repaired; USD is 99.98% of the shark file, so currency was ignored there.
  • Single random seeds and splits (seed 42); small differences (e.g. SMOTE vs class weights) are within fold-to-fold variation.
  • Many tests were run without multiplicity correction; with n ≈ 14.5k, p-values are almost always tiny, so effect sizes are emphasised.

Reproduce

pip install -r requirements.txt
git clone https://github.com/VIDA-NYU/LTS.git
DATA_DIR=LTS/data_use_cases python analysis.py   # writes results.json + figures/
python build_site.py                             # writes index.html
